::: {.learning-objectives}
## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Explain how growth in data, new technology, and changing professional expectations have reshaped the work accountants perform.
2. Distinguish descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive analytics and identify examples of each in financial accounting, managerial accounting, and auditing.
3. Describe the six stages of the accounting analytics workflow, from defining the question through communicating results.
4. Compare Excel, SQL, and Power BI and identify the workflow stages each tool supports best.
5. Describe the Charles River business, its table groups, and how operational activity reaches the general ledger.
:::

## Opening Scenario {.unnumbered}

You have just started a position as a staff accountant at Charles River, a mid-size home furnishings company in the greater Boston area. During your first week, the controller asks you to investigate why gross margins on the Furniture product line declined in the most recent quarter. She tells you the data you need is spread across several tables in the company's database, including sales orders, product cost records, and the general ledger. Your accounting coursework prepared you to interpret financial statements, calculate ratios, and apply standards, but you have never pulled data directly from a database, cleaned it for analysis, or built an interactive report that the management team can explore on their own. You realize that answering the controller's question will require more than accounting knowledge. It will require the ability to extract, prepare, analyze, and communicate data. This chapter introduces the analytical mindset and the toolkit you will develop throughout this book to handle exactly this kind of challenge.


## The Changing Landscape of Accounting Work

The accounting profession has always been built on data. Accountants record transactions, classify them into accounts, summarize them in financial statements, and interpret the results for stakeholders. For most of the profession's history, the volume of data involved in these tasks was manageable through manual methods and later through basic spreadsheets. A general ledger might contain a few thousand entries per year, and an auditor could review a reasonable portion of those entries by hand. That era has ended.

Modern organizations generate transaction data at a scale that makes manual review impractical. A single retail company may process millions of sales transactions per month, each one recorded with a timestamp, a product identifier, a customer identifier, a store location, a payment method, and a discount code. An enterprise resource planning system at a manufacturing firm captures not only financial transactions but also production orders, material movements, quality inspections, and employee time records. The data that accountants must work with has grown by orders of magnitude, and it continues to grow (Vasarhelyi et al., 2015).

This growth in data has created both a challenge and an opportunity for the profession. The challenge is that traditional methods of sampling and manual review cannot keep pace with the volume and complexity of modern datasets. An auditor who selects 50 transactions from a population of 500,000 is examining one hundredth of one percent of the available evidence. The opportunity is that the same technology that generates massive datasets also provides tools to analyze entire populations rather than small samples. Accountants who can use these tools effectively bring more evidence to their conclusions, identify patterns that sampling would miss, and deliver insights that go beyond compliance and reporting (Barr-Pulliam et al., 2022; Earley, 2015).

Automation is also changing the work itself. Software now performs many routine tasks, such as matching invoices to purchase orders and preparing standard reconciliations, and artificial intelligence tools, including generative AI, can draft analyses and flag unusual transactions in seconds. These tools have not removed the need for accountants. They shift the accountant's contribution toward framing the right questions, judging whether the underlying data is reliable, and exercising the professional judgment that software cannot supply (Kokina et al., 2025; Law & Shen, 2025). Early field evidence shows how this division of labor works. Among accountants using an AI-enabled accounting platform for small and medium-sized businesses, generative AI took over much of the routine data entry, and the accountants shifted their time toward client communication and quality review. They corrected the AI's classifications more often when the AI was less confident in them, and in a related experiment, relying on incorrect AI suggestions increased the risk of error (Choi & Xie, 2026). An accountant who understands how data is structured and analyzed is far better placed to use these tools well and to recognize when their output is wrong. The further reading at the end of this chapter follows these developments.

Professional bodies have recognized this shift and updated the competencies they expect. The American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) and the National Association of State Boards of Accountancy (NASBA) added accounting data analytics, digital acumen, and IT governance to the model curriculum for aspiring CPAs, and the CPA Exam that took effect in January 2024 places greater emphasis on technology (AICPA & NASBA, 2021). The Institute of Management Accountants (IMA) expanded its competency framework in 2025, with domains dedicated to data analytics and to emerging technology in accounting (IMA, 2025). Internationally, the International Accounting Education Standards Board (IAESB) revised its education standards to strengthen the information and communications technology competencies expected of professional accountants (IAESB, 2019). These developments signal that analytics is not a niche specialization within accounting. It is a core competency that every practitioner will need.

::: {.callout-tip .in-practice icon=false}
## In Practice
Analytics and technology skills remain difficult for finance organizations to develop and recruit. In a 2025 survey by the AICPA and the Chartered Institute of Management Accountants (CIMA), half of the 1,446 finance and accounting leaders and managers who responded worldwide named a lack of human capital, skills, and talent as the leading barrier to adopting new technology. Respondents also reported skills gaps in data and analytics; communication, influencing, and critical thinking; and business partnering (AICPA & CIMA, 2025). An analysis of Australian job listings that combined accounting and data analytics tasks found that employers wanted people who could extract insights from data, solve complex business problems, communicate and visualize findings, and use tools such as Excel, SQL, and Power BI (Askary & Askarany, 2024). Together, these findings suggest that accounting professionals increasingly need to combine traditional accounting expertise with analytical, technological, and communication skills.
:::

The purpose of this book is to help you develop these skills in a structured and practical way. You will learn to work with data using Microsoft Excel, SQL, and Microsoft Power BI, three tools that are widely used in practice. You will apply these tools to realistic accounting data drawn from the Charles River Accounting Dataset, a single integrated database that you will use throughout the entire book. And you will practice solving problems from the perspectives of financial accounting, managerial accounting, and auditing. By the end of this book, you will be able to extract data from a database, prepare it for analysis, summarize and model it, visualize the results, and communicate your findings to professional audiences.


## Defining Accounting Analytics

Analytics is the process of examining data to draw conclusions, identify patterns, and support decisions. In accounting, analytics applies this process to financial and operational data for purposes such as reporting, planning, control, and assurance. In this book, accounting analytics means extracting, preparing, analyzing, and visualizing accounting data to produce information that supports financial reporting, managerial decisions, and audit assurance.

Accounting analytics overlaps with several related terms you are likely to encounter. "Data analytics" is a broad term that encompasses analytical work in any domain, from marketing to healthcare to logistics. "Business intelligence" typically refers to the tools and infrastructure that organizations use to collect, store, and present data for operational and strategic decisions. "Big data" refers to datasets that are too large or complex for traditional data processing methods and is usually associated with cloud data platforms and distributed processing. Accounting analytics draws on all of these concepts but applies them specifically to the data, questions, and standards that define the accounting profession (Richins et al., 2017).

### Types of Analytics

A useful framework for understanding the scope of analytics divides it into four types: descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive. Each type answers a different question, and together they form a continuum of increasing analytical complexity, as @fig-01-01 shows. The types are not mutually exclusive. Most real-world accounting analytics projects involve more than one.

![The Analytics Continuum.](/visuals/svg/fig-01-01-analytics-continuum.svg){#fig-01-01 fig-alt="A horizontal diagram showing four stages from left to right: Descriptive Analytics (What happened?), Diagnostic Analytics (Why did it happen?), Predictive Analytics (What might happen?), and Prescriptive Analytics (What should we do?). An arrow beneath them indicates increasing analytical complexity, and each stage has an accounting example: revenue summary by quarter, drill-down of a margin decline, regression forecast of sales, and optimal product mix via Solver."}


**Descriptive analytics** answers the question "what happened?" It involves summarizing historical data to understand past performance, identify trends, and describe the current state of affairs. Descriptive analytics is the foundation of most accounting work. When a financial analyst prepares a comparative income statement showing revenue by product line for the past four quarters, that is descriptive analytics. When an auditor stratifies accounts receivable by aging bucket to assess the adequacy of the allowance for doubtful accounts, that is also descriptive analytics. The tools of descriptive analytics include aggregation, grouping, sorting, filtering, and basic statistical measures such as totals, averages, and counts.

In this book, descriptive analytics appears most prominently in the Excel chapters of Part II and the introductory SQL chapters of Part III. You will build PivotTables that summarize Charles River invoiced revenue by item group and quarter, write SQL queries that calculate average order values by customer, and create Power BI dashboards that display key performance indicators from the general ledger. These are all descriptive tasks, and they form the base on which more advanced analysis is built.

**Diagnostic analytics** answers the question "why did it happen?" It picks up where descriptive analytics leaves off, investigating the causes behind a result by drilling down into the details, comparing segments, and breaking a change into its components. The controller's question in the opening scenario is a diagnostic question. A descriptive summary can show that the gross margin on Furniture fell in the most recent quarter, but explaining why requires decomposing the decline into its drivers: lower selling prices, a shift in the mix of products sold, higher product costs, or some combination of the three. Diagnostic analytics is central to accounting work. Management accountants use it to explain variances from budget, and auditors use it to investigate unusual fluctuations identified during analytical procedures. The tools of diagnostic analytics include drill-down, variance decomposition, segment comparison, and tracing exceptions back to the transactions that caused them.

Diagnostic work appears throughout this book, wherever a summary raises a question that the underlying transactions can answer. In the Excel chapters, you will drill into PivotTables to locate the source of a change. In the SQL chapters, you will join tables to trace an unusual balance back to individual documents. In the Power BI chapters, you will build drill-through reports that let managers explore causes on their own.

**Predictive analytics** answers the question "what might happen?" It involves using historical data to make forecasts, estimate probabilities, and identify the factors that drive outcomes. Predictive analytics moves beyond explaining the past to projecting the future. When a management accountant builds a regression model to forecast next quarter's revenue based on historical trends, that is predictive analytics. When an auditor uses statistical analysis to set an expectation for an account balance and then compares the actual balance to the expectation as a substantive analytical procedure, that too involves prediction. The tools of predictive analytics include regression analysis, trend extrapolation, time series modeling, and classification techniques.

In this book, predictive analytics appears in the modeling work of the Excel chapters in Part II, in the SQL chapters of Part III, where period-over-period comparisons and trailing twelve-month measures reveal the trends on which expectations are built, and in the Power BI chapters of Part IV, where DAX time intelligence functions support rolling averages and year-over-year comparisons. You will build forecasting models using Charles River sales data, test how sensitive a promotion's payoff is to its assumptions with what-if tools, and set analytical expectations that mirror the procedures used in professional practice.

**Prescriptive analytics** answers the question "what should we do?" It involves using data analysis to recommend a course of action, often by optimizing an objective subject to constraints. Prescriptive analytics is the most advanced of the four types and is less common in current accounting practice than the others, although it is growing. When a cost accountant uses Excel's Solver tool to determine the optimal product mix that maximizes contribution margin given production capacity constraints, that is prescriptive analytics. When a tax advisor uses scenario modeling to recommend a filing strategy that minimizes a client's tax liability across multiple jurisdictions, that also has prescriptive elements.

This book introduces prescriptive analytics through optimization exercises in the Excel chapters of Part II, using Solver and Scenario Manager, and through the decisions that the case chapters of Part V ask you to recommend. The emphasis throughout the book, however, is on descriptive, diagnostic, and predictive analytics because these represent the analytical work that accounting professionals perform most frequently. Studies of management accountants, for example, find that their analytics work remains largely descriptive (Appelbaum et al., 2017; Spraakman et al., 2021).

::: {.callout-warning .watch-out icon=false}
## Watch out
It is tempting to assume that descriptive analytics is "basic" and that the goal is to reach prescriptive analytics as quickly as possible. In practice, most accounting analytics work is descriptive, and doing it well requires substantial skill. A poorly constructed summary can mislead decision makers just as easily as a sophisticated model can. The value of analytics lies not in its complexity but in the quality of the questions it answers and the rigor of the process behind it.
:::


## Analytics Across Accounting Roles

The demand for analytics skills comes from every area of the profession, and the applied exercises in this book are organized around three of them: financial accounting, managerial accounting, and auditing. Seeing how each area uses data helps explain why the skills in this book matter for your career, whichever path you choose.

In financial reporting, analytics supports the close, reconciliation, and disclosure processes. Reporting teams extract general ledger detail to reconcile subsidiary ledgers to control accounts, analyze fluctuations in account balances before the financial statements are issued, and validate the data that flows from many interconnected tables into the statements. A survey of finance professionals found that finance functions pursuing efficiency make greater use of both automation and analytics when their firms emphasize digitalization (Bedford et al., 2025). In small and medium-sized businesses, using generative AI to record and classify transactions has been associated with more detailed charts of accounts and a month-end close that finishes about a week sooner (Choi & Xie, 2026). Accountants who can access and analyze the data directly, rather than waiting for other departments to produce reports, can answer questions as they arise.

In managerial accounting, the accountant's role has expanded beyond preparer and verifier to include advisor and analyst. Organizations expect their accounting and finance teams to provide forward-looking analysis, scenario planning, and strategic insight, not just historical reports. Management accountants are asked to explain why results differ from plan, to forecast future performance under different assumptions, and to identify the operational drivers behind financial outcomes. These tasks require analytical skills that go beyond debits and credits (Appelbaum et al., 2017; Bedford et al., 2025). A survey of US firms found that broader data sources and a data-driven culture improved decision quality only where management accountants' data analytics skills were highly developed (Franke & Hiebl, 2023).

In auditing, analytics is changing the nature of audit evidence. The ability to test an entire population of transactions rather than a sample allows auditors to identify anomalies that sampling would miss, perform more precise risk assessments, and provide more relevant findings to audit committees. Auditing standards are adapting to this shift. In 2024, the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) amended its standards on audit evidence and on responses to the risks of material misstatement to clarify the auditor's responsibilities when using technology-assisted analysis, and the amendments took effect for audits of fiscal years beginning on or after December 15, 2025 (PCAOB, 2024). Internal auditors apply the same techniques to monitor controls and transactions continuously throughout the year.

Across all three areas, employers look for graduates who combine accounting knowledge with data skills. Studies of accounting job advertisements find employers asking for advanced spreadsheet skills and the ability to work with enterprise resource planning and cloud accounting systems, along with a growing demand for information and communication technology skills, especially in entry- and mid-level positions (Elo et al., 2026; Suarta et al., 2024). Audit firms report recruiting technology-savvy graduates and expect the auditors of the future to bring information technology and data analytics skills (Liew et al., 2022; Vitali & Giuliani, 2024). The ability to write a SQL query, build a PivotTable, or create an interactive dashboard can set you apart in a hiring process and open career paths that were once reserved for specialists in information systems or data science.

@tbl-01-01 shows how each of the four types of analytics appears in financial accounting, managerial accounting, and auditing, using examples drawn from the Charles River data you will analyze in this book.

| Type | Financial Accounting | Managerial Accounting | Auditing |
|---|---|---|---|
| Descriptive | Comparative income statement showing revenue by item group for the past four quarters | Product profitability ranking by item group based on standard cost and list price from the Item table | Stratification of Charles River sales invoices by aging bucket to evaluate the allowance for doubtful accounts |
| Diagnostic | Drill-down of a quarterly revenue shortfall by customer segment and item group to explain the change from the prior quarter | Decomposition of the decline in Furniture gross margin into price, volume, mix, and cost effects | Investigation of sales invoices dated before the goods were shipped to determine whether revenue was recorded in the wrong period |
| Predictive | Revenue forecast for the next fiscal quarter using trend extrapolation of historical Charles River sales data | Cost-volume-profit model projecting break-even points for the Furniture product line under three pricing scenarios | Regression-based expectation for monthly revenue used as a substantive analytical procedure |
| Prescriptive | Recommended sequence of period-end close tasks that minimizes the days needed to close, given staff availability | Product mix recommendation that maximizes total contribution margin across the four product families, subject to constraints on machine hours and raw material availability | Allocation of substantive testing hours across audit areas that minimizes residual risk within a given engagement budget |

::: {.callout-tip .in-practice icon=false}
## In Practice
The three-perspective exercise structure in this book reflects how analytics is used across the accounting profession. The same technique can serve different purposes depending on the role. A duplicate-payment analysis, for example, supports controls assurance in an audit context, vendor management in a procurement context, and cash flow review in a controllership context. Seeing these connections will help you understand why a single analytical skill has broad professional value.
:::


## The Accounting Analytics Workflow

Before learning specific tools, it is helpful to understand the general process that accounting analytics projects follow. Whether you are building a revenue summary in Excel, writing an audit query in SQL, or designing a dashboard in Power BI, the work progresses through the six stages shown in @fig-01-02. This book is organized around these stages, and the controller's question from the opening scenario shows how they fit together.

![The Accounting Analytics Workflow.](/visuals/svg/fig-01-02-analytics-workflow.svg){#fig-01-02 fig-alt="A process flowchart showing six stages in sequence: (1) Define the Question, (2) Identify and Access the Data, (3) Prepare and Clean the Data, (4) Analyze the Data, (5) Visualize and Present the Results, (6) Communicate Findings and Recommendations. Each stage includes a one-sentence description, and a note indicates which parts of the book develop each stage."}

The first stage is defining the question. Every analytics project begins with a clear statement of the problem or question to be addressed. In the opening scenario, the controller asked a specific question: why did gross margins on the Furniture product line decline in the most recent quarter? A well-defined question guides every subsequent decision, from which data to collect to which visualizations to create. Vague questions produce vague answers. The ability to translate a business concern into an analytical question is one of the most important skills an accountant can develop.

The second stage is identifying and accessing the data. Once the question is defined, you must determine which data is needed and where it resides. In many organizations, the relevant data is stored in databases that are part of the company's ERP system or accounting software, and accessing it may require writing SQL queries to extract the relevant tables and columns. In other cases, the data may be available in spreadsheet exports or flat files. To answer the controller's question, you would need invoiced sales by product and quarter, the cost of the products sold, and the general ledger accounts where revenue and cost of goods sold are recorded. Chapters 2 and 3 prepare you for this stage by explaining how accounting data is structured and stored within the Charles River database.

The third stage is preparing and cleaning the data. Raw data almost always contains problems that must be resolved before analysis can begin. Missing values, duplicate records, inconsistent formatting, and incorrect data types are common in accounting datasets. Before calculating margins, for example, you would confirm that every invoice line is linked to a product and that returns and credit memos are treated consistently. Data preparation is often the most time-consuming stage of an analytics project, and it is also among the most important, because analysis performed on dirty data produces unreliable results. The Excel chapters of Part II and the SQL chapters of Part III both teach data preparation techniques.

The fourth stage is analyzing the data. This is where you apply techniques such as summarization, comparison, trend analysis, regression, and anomaly detection to answer the question defined in the first stage. The choice of technique depends on the question and the type of data available. For the controller, you would calculate gross margin by quarter for each item group and then decompose the Furniture decline into its volume, mix, price, and cost effects, which is diagnostic analysis. Analysis techniques are taught in Excel in Part II, in SQL in Part III, and in Power BI in Part IV.

The fifth stage is visualizing and presenting the results. Data visualization transforms analytical results into visual formats that audiences can interpret quickly and accurately. A well-designed chart, table, or dashboard communicates the answer to the original question more effectively than a spreadsheet full of numbers. In one experiment, managers who received graphs alongside tables made better performance evaluations than managers who received tables alone (Hirsch et al., 2015). A single chart showing Furniture margin by quarter, with the contribution of each driver highlighted, would let the controller see the answer at a glance. Part IV covers visualization principles and teaches you to build interactive reports and dashboards in Power BI.

The sixth stage is communicating findings and recommendations. The final product of an analytics project is not a spreadsheet or a dashboard but a communication to decision makers. That communication might take the form of a written memorandum to an audit committee, a presentation to management, or an interactive report that stakeholders can explore. In the opening scenario, it would be a short memorandum to the controller that explains why the Furniture margin fell and what management might do about it. The ability to translate analytical results into clear, professional language is essential. In a survey of accounting professionals, respondents ranked data interpretation and communication above any individual technical or statistical skill for new graduates (Brink & Stoel, 2019). You will practice this ability throughout the book in the applied exercises and comprehensive cases, each of which asks for a written interpretation alongside the technical work.

::: {.callout-note .connecting-dots icon=false}
## Connecting the Dots
The six-stage workflow described here is not unique to accounting. It closely parallels the data analysis process described in data science and business intelligence literature (Provost & Fawcett, 2013). What makes accounting analytics distinctive is not the process itself but the data it works with (financial and operational transactions), the questions it addresses (reporting, control, assurance), and the professional standards that govern the work (GAAP, GAAS, IMA ethical standards). Throughout this book, the workflow provides the thread that connects every chapter and every tool.
:::

## The Tools of This Book

This book uses three tools: Microsoft Excel, SQL (Structured Query Language), and Microsoft Power BI. They were selected because they are widely used in accounting practice, they are accessible to readers without programming backgrounds, and together they cover the full analytics workflow from data access through communication. Each tool has distinct strengths, and part of becoming an effective analyst is knowing which tool fits which task.

Microsoft Excel is the most widely used analytical tool in accounting. Its grid of rows and columns makes it natural for organizing data, building calculations, and preparing workpapers, and features such as PivotTables, lookup functions, Power Query, and Solver extend it well beyond simple arithmetic. Excel is strongest for ad hoc analysis, financial modeling, and work that a reviewer needs to trace cell by cell. It becomes harder to manage when data grows to hundreds of thousands of rows or spans many related tables.

SQL is the standard language for retrieving and combining data stored in relational databases. Rather than copying data into a spreadsheet, you write a query that describes the data you want, and the database returns it. SQL is strongest when data is large, when it spans multiple related tables that must be joined, and when a procedure needs to be saved and run again, as with a recurring audit test. In this book, you will write SQL against a SQLite version of the Charles River database.

Microsoft Power BI is a business intelligence platform for building data models, interactive reports, and dashboards. It connects to multiple data sources, relates tables to one another in a data model, and uses a formula language called DAX to define calculated measures. Power BI is strongest when results must be shared with an audience that wants to explore the data on its own, such as department managers filtering a dashboard to their own cost center.

@tbl-01-02 summarizes how the three tools compare.

| Tool | Strongest For | Typical Accounting Uses | Main Workflow Stages | Where in This Book |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Microsoft Excel | Ad hoc analysis, modeling, and workpapers a reviewer can trace | Reconciliations, PivotTable summaries, forecasting models, audit workpapers | Prepare, analyze | Part II |
| SQL | Large datasets that span related tables, and procedures that must be repeated | Extracting ledger detail, joining documents across a business cycle, population-level audit tests | Access, prepare, analyze | Part III |
| Microsoft Power BI | Interactive reporting for audiences that explore the data themselves | Financial and operational dashboards, budget-versus-actual reports, audit monitoring | Analyze, visualize, communicate | Part IV |

SQL handles most of the work in data access and preparation, and much of the analysis when the data is large or spread across related tables. Excel dominates preparation and analysis. Power BI takes the lead in visualization and presentation. All three tools contribute to the communication of results.

## Connecting the Dots
Part V of this book integrates all three tools using the full Charles River database. Its chapters are comprehensive cases that prescribe no fixed order of tools. A step that needs a whole population or a join across tables goes to SQL, a schedule or a model that needs judgment goes to Excel, and a result that a reader needs to explore goes to Power BI. This mirrors how analytics projects work in practice, where no single tool handles every stage of the workflow.
:::

## The Charles River Accounting Dataset

This book is built around one integrated dataset that you will use in every chapter. The Charles River Accounting Dataset follows a single fictional mid-size home furnishings company in the greater Boston area that designs and sells furniture, lighting, textiles, and decorative accessories through wholesale and direct-to-business channels, manufactures selected product lines in-house, and operates an interior design services practice that bills customers by the hour. Working with one company throughout the book means you learn one business deeply rather than several superficially, and every chapter builds on the same data environment. The About the Dataset section in the front matter introduces the company and its business cycles in more detail.

The database is organized into table groups, each covering one area of business activity, from customer orders and supplier payments through manufacturing, payroll, and general ledger posting. @tbl-01-03 summarizes the groups, the key tables in each, and their primary accounting uses. The book introduces these groups progressively, starting with the most accessible tables in the early Excel chapters and expanding into the more complex groups as your skills develop. @fig-01-04 shows how the groups connect through the general ledger, where the financial activity of every business cycle is ultimately posted. Complete documentation of every table and column is available on the dataset website.

| Table Group | Key Tables | Primary Accounting Use |
|---|---|---|
| Accounting Core | Account, JournalEntry, GLEntry | Financial reporting, audit analytics, period-close analysis |
| Order-to-Cash (O2C) | Customer, SalesOrder, SalesOrderLine, Shipment, SalesInvoice, CashReceipt, ServiceEngagement | Revenue analysis, receivables management, design services margin analysis, sales commissions |
| Procure-to-Pay (P2P) | PurchaseRequisition, PurchaseOrder, GoodsReceipt, PurchaseInvoice, DisbursementPayment | Purchasing analytics, three-way matching, vendor evaluation, duplicate payment detection |
| Manufacturing | BillOfMaterial, WorkOrder, MaterialIssue, ProductionCompletion, WorkOrderClose | Standard versus actual cost analysis, production performance, material usage variance |
| Payroll and Time | TimeClockEntry, LaborTimeEntry, PayrollRegister, PayrollPayment | Labor cost analysis, payroll compliance testing, workforce analytics |
| Fixed Assets and Financing | FixedAsset, FixedAssetEvent, DebtAgreement, DebtScheduleLine | Depreciation analysis, asset lifecycle tracking, debt amortization |
| Master Data | Item, Warehouse, Employee | Shared reference data for products, locations, and people across all groups |
| Organizational Planning | CostCenter, Budget, BudgetLine | Departmental budgetary control, responsibility accounting, budget-versus-actual analysis |
| Demand Planning and MRP | DemandForecast, InventoryPolicy, SupplyPlanRecommendation, MaterialRequirementPlan, RoughCutCapacityPlan | Demand forecasting, inventory planning, production planning |

: Charles River Table Groups {#tbl-01-03}

The design services practice does not have a table group of its own. Its tables, such as ServiceEngagement, ServiceTimeEntry, and ServiceBillingLine, sit within the Order-to-Cash group, giving you a service revenue cycle alongside the product revenue cycle.

![Charles River High-Level Architecture Diagram.](/visuals/svg/fig-01-04-charles-river-architecture.svg){#fig-01-04 fig-alt="A diagram showing the Charles River table groups as labeled blocks around the Accounting Core, with GLEntry at the center. Dashed arrows show how each business cycle posts its financial activity to the general ledger: Order-to-Cash through invoices, shipments, and cash receipts; Procure-to-Pay through goods receipts, invoices, and payments; Manufacturing through material issues, production completions, and work order closes; Payroll and Time through payroll summaries, payments, and remittances; and Fixed Assets and Financing through purchase invoices for asset acquisitions and journal entries for depreciation, debt service, and disposals. Design Services appears as a dashed block within Order-to-Cash. Heavier solid arrows show that Master Data, Organizational Planning, and Demand Planning and MRP connect to the Accounting Core through shared keys such as ItemID, EmployeeID, CostCenterID, and AccountID."}

Two features make it possible to connect the groups. First, shared key columns link related tables across groups. ItemID connects product-level activity in sales, purchasing, manufacturing, and planning. AccountID connects the general ledger, budgets, and the chart of accounts. EmployeeID connects payroll, time records, and service engagements, and CostCenterID connects operating activity, labor, and budgets by organizational unit. Second, every entry in the GLEntry table records the source document that created it. The SourceDocumentType column identifies the kind of document, such as a SalesInvoice, a Shipment, or a JournalEntry. The SourceDocumentID column identifies the specific document, and the SourceLineID column identifies the line within that document when the posting comes from a single line. Together, these three columns let you trace a ledger posting back to the business event behind it. This source-to-ledger traceability is one of the most valuable features of the dataset, and you will use it repeatedly in this book.

Two visual examples illustrate the structure you will work with throughout the book. @fig-01-05 traces the Order-to-Cash cycle from a sales order through shipment, invoice, and cash receipt. Each stage creates records in its own tables, and the shipment, the invoice, the cash receipt, and its application to the invoice each post to the general ledger. @fig-01-06 follows a single posting in the opposite direction. The GLEntry row that records $688.42 of furniture revenue names its source through SourceDocumentType, SourceDocumentID, and SourceLineID, which lead back to invoice SI-2025-007947 and its line for two Alder desks. Its AccountID leads to account 4010, Sales Revenue - Furniture. Chapter 3 explains how columns like these connect tables, and Tutorial 3.2 traces the same invoice through every table it touches. Every financial event in the database is ultimately posted to GLEntry, making it the single source of truth for the company's financial position. Operational records that have no financial effect, such as open sales orders or budgets, remain outside the ledger.

![Simplified O2C Process Flow.](/visuals/svg/fig-01-05-o2c-process-flow.svg){#fig-01-05 fig-alt="A two-row flowchart of the Order-to-Cash path. In the first row, a Customer places a SalesOrder, which has SalesOrderLines that draw product details from the Item table in Master Data. The path continues in the second row: a Shipment fulfills the order, a SalesInvoice bills it, the customer pays through a CashReceipt, and CashReceiptApplication matches the receipt to the invoices it pays. Dashed arrows from the shipment, the invoice, the cash receipt, and the application lead down to GLEntry in the Accounting Core, labeled COGS and inventory, revenue and AR, cash, and clears AR."}

![One Ledger Posting Traced to Its Source.](/visuals/svg/fig-01-06-ledger-posting-trace.svg){#fig-01-06 fig-alt="A GLEntry row shown as a list of columns and values: GLEntryID 126312, PostingDate 2025-03-05, AccountID 42, a credit of $688.42, SourceDocumentType SalesInvoice, SourceDocumentID 7947, and SourceLineID 10645. A solid arrow labeled which account leads from AccountID to the Account row for 4010 Sales Revenue - Furniture. Dashed arrows labeled which table, which row, and which line lead from the three source columns to the SalesInvoice row for SI-2025-007947 and to invoice line 10645, which bills two units of item FUR-DSK-0075 at $344.21 for $688.42."}

::: {.callout-warning .watch-out icon=false}
## Watch out
The Charles River dataset is a fictional company created for educational purposes. It is designed to illustrate realistic data structures and analytical challenges, but it does not represent the full complexity or messiness of real-world data. Real ERP systems may contain hundreds of tables, custom fields, and data quality problems that exceed what you will encounter in this dataset. The skills you learn here will transfer to real-world environments, but you should expect that professional practice will require additional adaptation and judgment.
:::

{{< include _tutorial-01.qmd >}}

## How This Book Is Organized

This book is organized into five parts that follow the analytics workflow and introduce the tools in a sequence designed for readers with no prior analytics or programming experience. As @fig-01-08 shows, the parts also introduce the Charles River table groups progressively, starting with the most accessible tables and expanding as your skills develop.

**Part I, Foundations of Accounting Analytics**, establishes the conceptual groundwork. You are in Part I now. Chapter 2 will teach you to think critically about accounting data, including its types, sources, and quality, and Chapter 3 will introduce the relational database model and show you how the Charles River database is organized. A comprehensive case at the end of Part I then asks you to use all three chapters to get the data ready for the controller's question from the opening scenario.

**Part II, Accounting Analytics with Excel**, teaches you to use Excel as an analytical tool, from data organization and cleaning through summarization, modeling, and audit-specific analytics. It works primarily with the Order-to-Cash and Accounting Core groups and the Item table from Master Data, and it draws on the planning and purchasing tables for budgeting and audit tests.

**Part III, Accounting Analytics with SQL**, teaches you to query relational databases directly, from the basic SELECT statement through joins, aggregation, window functions, and audit analytics queries. It expands into the Procure-to-Pay and Manufacturing groups, where relational joins become essential.

**Part IV, Data Visualization and Power BI**, teaches you to build interactive reports and dashboards, from visualization principles through data modeling with DAX and full dashboard design, using data models that span multiple table groups.

**Part V, Integrated and Applied Topics**, applies the full toolkit in three comprehensive cases: one in financial reporting, one in managerial accounting, and one in auditing. Each case requires you to move between Excel, SQL, and Power BI within a single project, choosing the tool each step calls for, just as you would in professional practice. Parts II to IV also close with a comprehensive case, as Part I does.

![Book Organization Map.](/visuals/svg/fig-01-08-book-organization-map.svg){#fig-01-08 fig-alt="A visual roadmap showing the five parts of the book as a progression from left to right. Part I (Foundations, all groups at overview) leads to Part II (Excel, sales and ledger tables, then planning and purchasing), Part III (SQL, expands into P2P and Manufacturing), and Part IV (Power BI, cross-group models), which converge into Part V (Integrated and Applied Topics, three comprehensive cases that use all three tools and all table groups). A note indicates that a comprehensive case closes each of Parts I to IV."}

## Looking Ahead

This chapter introduced the concept of accounting analytics, defined the four types of analytics, examined how analytics supports each area of the profession, and outlined the workflow that connects every chapter. It also introduced the tools and the Charles River dataset you will use throughout the book. You will answer the controller's question from the opening scenario in Chapter 6, with Excel. By the time you reach the case chapters of Part V, you will be able to answer questions like it with all three tools, choosing for each step the tool that fits: SQL to extract and reconcile the invoice and cost data, Excel to model it, and Power BI to present your findings.

In the next chapter, you will take a closer look at accounting data itself. You will learn to distinguish different data types, identify common data quality problems, and understand why the quality of your data determines the quality of your analysis. The skills you begin building in Chapter 2 will support everything that follows.
